Wicked. Wicked is a 2003 musical by composer-lyricist Stephen Schwartz, based on Gregory Maguire's 1995 novel, that retells the story of the Wizard of Oz from the Wicked Witch of the West's perspective. It became a cultural juggernaut, exploring how villainy is constructed and innocence corrupted, while delivering soaring melodies and a powerful central friendship that resonates across generations.

Schwartz, who also wrote Godspell and Pippin, transforms Maguire's revisionist novel into a story centered on the friendship between Elphaba, the future Wicked Witch, and Glinda, the Good Witch. The musical asks fundamental questions: how do people become wicked, and whose version of history gets told? It reframes the Wicked Witch as a victim of propaganda and unjust systems.

"Defying Gravity" is Elphaba's anthem of defiant self-determination, featuring a technically demanding vocal performance. It became one of the most iconic musical theatre moments of the twenty-first century. "For Good" is the emotional finale in which Glinda and Elphaba reflect on how they've changed each other, providing catharsis and underscoring the show's thesis about the power of friendship and understanding.

The score blends contemporary pop sensibilities with classic musical theatre orchestration, with melodies designed to be singable yet emotionally complex. The lyrics employ intricate rhyme schemes and metrical sophistication that match the show's intellectual depth.

The show premiered in New York in 2003 and became the highest-grossing musical production of all time, with global success and a record-breaking 2024 film adaptation. Its cultural reach speaks to Schwartz's sophisticated approach to melody and narrative.
